text:
The last thing Maya remembered was the machine dying in her garage. Then she was lying face down in wet grass with some cow staring at her like she'd done something deeply wrong.

She sat up. No power lines. No roads. Just a muddy track and a stone wall, and beyond it a tower with a banner she didn't recognize. Her phone was dead, no signal anyway. She was a physics grad student in a hoodie standing in what was obviously the Middle Ages.

"Marvelous," she muttered. "Really just marvelous."

This kid appeared at the wall staring at her sneakers, ran off shouting, and ten minutes later she was surrounded by villagers with pitchforks and some priest ready to do an exorcism. Her accent didn't help. Her clothes definitely didn't help. She kept hearing the word "witch."

So she did the only thing she could think of. Held up her dead phone like a holy relic and said as calmly as she could, "I come in peace."

Long pause. Then the blacksmith, this huge guy named Edric, laughed. "She talks like a goose," he said, "but she's not been struck by lightning. Let her stay in the barn."

The next few weeks were humbling. Maya could code and explain relativity but couldn't light a fire without a lighter. She failed at milking the cow, burned the porridge, fell into the river trying to wash clothes. The villagers figured she was a foreign noblewoman who'd lost her mind and kind of felt bad for her. Edric's wife Hild taught her to spin wool. The boy Tom taught her which berries wouldn't kill her.

Then she figured out how to be useful. Remembered a documentary, told them to boil their water and dig the latrine far from the well. When sickness hit the neighboring village months later, nobody in theirs got sick. They stopped calling her a witch. Called her "the clever one."

She spent every spare hour trying to rebuild her machine from memory, scratching equations on slate. The problem was she'd left the crystal oscillator in her own century and nothing she could forge would work.

One autumn evening watching smoke from the chimneys she realized she wasn't unhappy. Cold hands, rough skin, would've traded a finger for pizza and a hot shower. But she belonged somewhere. That was new.

Then Edric brought her something he found digging: a piece of smoky quartz. Crude, but quartz is a crystal, and quartz resonates. Maya stared at it for a long time.

"What is it?" Tom asked.

"A way home maybe." She looked around at everyone by the fire. "Or maybe a reason not to go."

The bell jangled and this half-orc in dented armor dragged a wet sack into Gruntle's Loans & Curios.

"Morning, Brakka," said Odalys, not looking up from the ledger. She was the owner, a gnome with glasses thick enough to start fires. "That better not be what I think."

"It's loot! Dragon's tooth. Fresh."

Odalys looked. Pulled it out with two fingers, tapped it on the counter, sniffed it. "This is a horse's tooth. A big horse."

"It was a dragon."

"It was a Clydesdale. Ten coppers."

"Ten? I fought—"

"You fought a horse." She sighed. "Fine. Twelve because you've never lied about the little things."

Brakka squinted. "That's a compliment right?"

Then the bell rang again. This slim elf in a velvet cloak set down a small ring like a magician.

"Ring of Boundless Fortune. Mildly cursed."

Odalys put on a second pair of glasses over the first. She turned the ring, watched the stone glow, felt her hand start to itch. "Mildly?"

"Bad luck streak. Brief."

"How brief?"

"Weeks. Maybe seasons."

"Forty gold."

"It's worth four hundred!"

"It's worth four hundred to someone who hates me, which honestly is a long list. Sixty, and you tell nobody I bought it."

The elf looked at the door where apparently someone angry was waiting. "Sixty-five and I'll leave through the back."

"Deal."

They shook on it. Odalys dropped the ring in a lead-lined drawer marked DO NOT, and the drawer rattled in disagreement.

Brakka, still holding twelve coppers, cleared her throat. "Uh, Odalys? Can I buy something back?"

"The tooth?"

"No. The sword. The one that sings."

From the back room came a faint melody, some mournful thing about lost love. It hadn't stopped for six days.

"Brakka," Odalys said slowly, "I'll sell it back for exactly what I paid. And if you tell anyone I'll put it in your bedroll."

Brakka grinned and slapped down five gold. "You're a hard woman."

"I'm a pawnbroker," said Odalys. "It's the same thing with receipts."

Here's a different ending.

Ted stood on the platform at Farhampton watching the 3:15 pull in. Rain on the roof. He'd been telling this story to his kids for nine years and finally got what it was actually about.

"Dad," Penny said, arms crossed, "you talked about Aunt Robin the whole time. You know that right?"

"Yeah," said Ted. "But wait."

He turned. On the other platform stood a woman with a yellow umbrella, bass case against her leg, soaked and laughing at something on her phone.

He'd thought this would end at a wedding. It ended with Tracy at a rainy station, the first time he heard her voice asking about the umbrella. Seven months with her was worth more than all the planning before.

In this version Tracy lived. The doctors caught it early and she got six more years, then twelve, then twenty. Robin got her career. He and Barney stayed married because he loved her and finally knew how to say so.

Ted never needed the blue French horn. Kept it on the shelf as a reminder of a guy who thought love meant one big gesture.

"Dad?" Luke said.

"Sorry kids." He grinned. "Just thinking about the best day of my life."

The woman across the tracks looked up and waved.

Ted waved back. For the first time the story felt done.

I'm one of the last Guardian Bears to retire and they asked me to tell the story of the Harrowgate Incident.

Back then I was with a boy named Thomas Whitlock, six years old, in a narrow room at the top of a house on Pell Street. Been with him since his first birthday. I was brown, worn at the left ear, had one glass eye and one button. These things don't matter for the work.

The rule is simple: monsters beneath the bed can't be defeated, only deterred. They're afraid of a stuffed animal's quiet attention. We hold the line. That's it.

That night his mother turned off the lamp at eight-thirty. By nine I heard it—dry scraping on floorboards. The signature of claws. I didn't panic. I settled my weight against the pillow and kept my good eye on the gap at the bed's edge.

Then something enormous exhaled under the mattress. The springs shivered. Thomas whispered "Bear?" I didn't answer because the rules say not to, but I leaned closer to his cheek and he went quiet.

Then the creature made its mistake. A long grey finger curled around the bedsheet. I'd been trained for this. I didn't move. I made my stillness absolute—the kind only a bear can do. The kind that says nothing here is afraid of you and nothing here will leave.

The finger hesitated. It pulled back. Long silence. Then the scraping went across the floor, down the stairs, out into the night.

By dawn Thomas was asleep, one hand on my worn ear. He never knew what happened. That's the rule.

I've been on a shelf beside a window for a long time now and Thomas is grown with a daughter of his own. Last winter I saw a new bear in her arms. Our eyes met briefly. I was satisfied. The line's in good hands.

Contemporary dance blends modern dance, jazz, ballet, release techniques and improvisation. It came together in the mid-twentieth century and keeps evolving.

Unlike classical ballet with its strict positions and upright posture, contemporary dance is fluid and versatile. Dancers work with gravity instead of against it—floor work, falls, rolls, spirals, weight shifts. Movement can be grounded, sharp or flowing within a single piece. The torso is way more expressive than in ballet.

Key stuff:
- **Emotional themes.** Pieces explore identity, relationships, politics, abstract ideas.
- **Floor work.** Using breath, momentum, muscle relaxation for natural movement.
- **Improvisation.** Choreographers develop movement through experimentation.
- **Any music.** Classical, pop, electronic, ambient, or silence.
- **Footwear:** Barefoot or light shoes.

Martha Graham, Merce Cunningham, Pina Bausch, Twyla Tharp shaped the form. These days it shows up on dance competition shows like *So You Think You Can Dance*.

text:
Doing a school exchange is one of the most valuable things a student can do. Sure it costs money and it's hard, but the benefits outweigh the problems.

You get exposed to a different culture. Living abroad forces you to adapt to different customs, food, different ways of thinking. Reading about it in a textbook is nothing like living it. You build empathy and lose stereotypes—increasingly important in a globalized world.

Language learning is huge. Classroom can only go so far but immersion makes you practice constantly—shops, lectures, friends. Most exchange students come back with fluency that would've taken years otherwise.

You also grow as a person. Managing unfamiliar situations, solving problems alone, dealing with homesickness—you become more confident, resilient, self-reliant. This helps later with studies and careers.

From an academic angle, exchanges are valuable. You get exposed to different teaching methods and courses unavailable at home. Employers value international experience too.

But there are real drawbacks. It's expensive and not every family can afford it. Some students struggle academically or feel isolated if their language isn't good. Scholarships and support programs help but they don't solve everything.

Overall, exchanges offer valuable opportunities for cultural understanding, language learning, personal development, career growth. They take preparation and resources but students should take the chance if they can, and schools should make them as accessible as possible.

Subject: Direct trade confirmations

Hi everyone,

Last week's review brought up a process issue. Some direct trades were agreed on the phone and confirmation only existed in someone's head or a quick chat. This has created confusion twice and I want to tighten things up.

When two parties agree a trade by voice there's no record unless you create one. If the other side later remembers the price or quantity or settlement date differently, we have nothing to point to. This exposes us to disputes, operational costs, and compliance issues.

Starting Monday, for every direct trade agreed verbally:

- **Use the recorded line.** Direct trades on recorded lines whenever possible. If you're on a mobile or in a meeting, call back on the recorded line to confirm.
- **Read back the key terms.** Say the instrument, side, quantity, price, trade date and settlement date to the counterparty, wait for yes.
- **Send written confirmation within 30 minutes.** Email or chat restating terms to the counterparty and copy operations.
- **Log the trade immediately.** Enter it in the blotter before moving on with a note it was verbal.

If anything's unclear or the counterparty disputes something, flag it to me right away.

This adds a few minutes per trade but saves way more time avoiding errors. Happy to walk through it if you want. I'll share a one-page checklist tomorrow.

Thanks,
Karen

text:
People answer "42" because of Douglas Adams's *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy*. It's become this internet joke—a way to dodge philosophy's biggest questions while sounding clever.

**Where it comes from**

In the story, hyper-intelligent beings build this enormous supercomputer called Deep Thought to calculate the "Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything." After seven and a half million years of computation it spits out: 42. Everyone's baffled. Deep Thought explains that the answer's meaningless because nobody actually knew what the question was. So they build a second computer—Earth—to figure out the question, but it gets destroyed minutes before finishing.

**Why it's funny**

It works on multiple levels. It parodies humanity's hunger for one neat answer to existence. The number is deliberately random and mundane, which deflates the grandiosity. It also points out a real thing: the quality of an answer depends on the question. If you don't know what you're asking, even a precise answer is useless.

Adams was also poking fun at how people treat computers like oracles, expecting profound truths through sheer processing power.

**Hidden meaning?**

Fans have looked for one. 42 is the ASCII code for asterisk. It equals 101010 in binary. Some point to cricket laws or the angle of a rainbow. Adams rejected all of it. He picked the number casually sitting at his desk and wanted something that sounded plain and unremarkable.

**Why people say it**

Today "42" works as a shared joke among programmers, scientists, sci-fi fans. Saying it means you know the reference and you're not taking the question seriously. Google's calculator returns 42 for "the answer to life, the universe and everything." Fans celebrate Towel Day May 25. It shows up in countless games, shows, software.

There's also something philosophically nice about the joke. Maybe the point is meaning isn't something you calculate. You have to decide the questions first, and the search itself might matter more than any number you find.

Every generation complains about the one after them. Parents complain about teenagers, grandparents about their grandchildren. I hear it all the time as a high school student. I don't think young people today are less respectful though. We just show respect differently and older people sometimes don't see it.

Yeah some things changed. Students used to stand when a teacher came in, called adults "sir" and "madam." Now a lot of us call teachers by first names, talk to adults more casually. Feels disrespectful to some older people. But casual isn't rude. It just reflects a culture that values openness and equality over strict hierarchy.

Young people show respect through actions too. Tons of teenagers volunteer at nursing homes, help elderly neighbors, teach grandparents how to video call. These things take patience and kindness. They're not as visible as formal manners but they're real care.

I'm not saying some young people don't behave badly. Some are rude to teachers, impatient with elders, glued to phones at dinner. But this has always happened. Every era had disrespectful people. It'd be unfair to judge a whole generation by the worst examples. There are also older people who dismiss young people without listening.

Technology changes how generations interact. Social media means young people spend more time with peers than family. Creates distance but it's not disrespect. It's just lack of shared experience, which conversation can fix.

Respect should go both ways. If older people listen to young voices and young people listen to experience, both sides understand each other better.

Young people today aren't less respectful. We express it differently, and with a bit more understanding from everyone, the gap gets smaller.

**Is it ethical to use animals in research?**

Every medicine you take was probably tested on an animal. So is it right to use animals for humans? I think yes, but only with strict rules and alternatives whenever possible.

The main argument for animal research is human health benefits. The polio vaccine, insulin, heart surgery—all developed with animal studies. Animals share biological features with us so scientists can see how treatments affect a living body in ways petri dishes can't. Millions are alive because of this.

But the opposition has strong points. Animals feel pain, fear, distress like we do. Many think it's wrong to make a creature suffer, especially when it can't consent. Plus animals aren't humans, so drugs that work on mice often fail in people. So some animal suffering doesn't lead anywhere useful.

The best approach is the "three Rs": replace animals with other methods when possible, reduce the number used, refine experiments to cause less pain. Scientists can use computer models and lab-grown tissues for some tests now. Governments should require ethics committees to review every experiment.

Using animals in research can be justified when necessary to save lives but it shouldn't be done carelessly. If scientists treat animals with respect and keep searching for better options, we protect both human health and our values.

Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in **1492**, landing October 12 on an island in the Bahamas the Lucayans called Guanahani. He renamed it San Salvador. Historians still debate which island exactly—Samana Cay and present-day San Salvador are the main candidates.

Columbus was a Genoese navigator who believed he could reach Asia by sailing west. After Portugal turned him down he got support from Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand, who financed the expedition. He sailed from Spain August 3, 1492 with three ships: the Nina, Pinta, Santa Maria. After stops in the Canary Islands the fleet spent over a month crossing the ocean.

After landing in the Bahamas, Columbus explored several islands including Cuba and Hispaniola. He thought he'd reached Asia's outskirts, which is why he called them the Indies and why indigenous people got called "Indians." The Santa Maria ran aground off Hispaniola on Christmas Day, and its wood built a small settlement named La Navidad. Columbus returned to Spain in early 1493 with plants, gold ornaments and several captive Taino people.

Columbus made three more trips in 1493, 1498 and 1502. During these voyages he explored more of the Caribbean and reached coasts of Central and South America. He never accepted he'd found a new continent.

Columbus wasn't the first from the Eastern Hemisphere to reach the Americas. Norse explorers led by Leif Erikson settled briefly at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland around 1000. Indigenous peoples lived there for thousands of years before either.

But the 1492 voyage started sustained contact between Europe and the Americas. This had enormous consequences—exchange of crops and animals, disease that devastated indigenous populations, start of European colonization. Columbus's legacy is widely debated now, with historians discussing both his navigational achievements and the violence and enslavement that followed.

Day one, I tried to ruin everything.

I'd won the election by basically nothing and woke up in the residence realizing I'd made a huge mistake. I didn't want to be in charge of anything.

So I made a plan. If I couldn't resign, I'd get myself thrown out.

First I announced on live TV that the national budget would be balanced by selling unused federal parking lots. Everyone laughed. Then economists ran the numbers and discovered the government owned several thousand acres of empty asphalt in prime city centers. The lots sold for billions. Developers built housing. Rents dropped. My approval rating went up six points.

Fine. Step two.

I declared "Do Nothing Wednesday" where all non-essential offices close and everyone goes outside. I expected impeachment calls immediately. Instead a study came out showing a surge in volunteer work, neighborhood gatherings, sleep. Hospitals reported fewer stress visits. A cereal company put my face on a box.

I got more desperate. Appointed my barber as Secretary of Commerce because he once described his business model and it sounded like a scam. It wasn't. Just a really good business model. He cut red tape the way he cuts hair—quick and without apologizing. Small businesses filed paperwork in an afternoon.

I tried insulting the opposition in a speech. Called them "a committee of very stubborn geese." Geese became their mascot. The first bipartisan bill in ten years passed because both sides wanted to prove they weren't geese.

Then I tried the big one. Pardoned a turkey, then pardoned the entire turkey industry's outstanding fines if they fixed their wastewater systems. Rivers got cleaner. Farmers sent thank-you notes with photos.

By autumn my approval rating was sixty-eight percent. Crowds chanted my name. A congressman I'd tried to enrage by wearing mismatched socks to the State of the Union gave me a standing ovation, mostly because he'd started wearing mismatched socks too.

That night I sat in the Oval Office staring at portraits of presidents who'd actually wanted the job.

"I just wanted to go home," I told the room.

Lincoln's portrait looked sympathetic.

But everything I'd broken was working. And somewhere in the building my chief of staff was laughing.

I picked up the phone. "Draft the reelection papers. And please, someone, find me a bigger scandal."

Hey everyone—a bunch of you asked me about the bread pudding from last month's lunch, so here it is. It's super easy and feeds a crowd.

Ingredients:
6 cups cubed day-old bread (brioche or french bread work)
2 cups whole milk
1 cup heavy cream
3 eggs
3/4 cup sugar
2 tsp vanilla
1 tsp cinnamon
1/2 cup raisins (optional)
3 tbsp melted butter

Steps:
1. Preheat to 350°F, butter a 9x13 dish
2. Whisk milk, cream, eggs, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon together
3. Toss bread and raisins in the dish, pour mixture over, soak 15 min
4. Drizzle with melted butter, bake 40-45 min until golden and set
5. Serve warm, tastes good with caramel or vanilla sauce

Makes it the night before if you want. Let me know if you need substitutions for stuff.

Hope it turns out well—Marcus

This problem comes up all the time in statistics—how confident are you that your hypothesis about a region actually has the true value? Phylogenetics and clustering use the multiscale bootstrap a lot. It resamples at different sample sizes and extrapolates back to n-1, and the AU p-value it gives is pretty useful in practice, but what it actually means statistically? Nobody really knew.

We framed it in selective inference—when you pick your hypothesis from the data you observe, you need to correct your inference. Turns out the AU p-value can be read as a selective inference p-value and controls type-I error correctly conditional on the selection. We also worked out some higher-order corrections using geometry of the region boundary curvature that give better accuracy for regions with smooth nonlinear boundaries.

You can see how bootstrap probability, AU p-values, and selective inference p-values all connect—they just differ in how they handle selection. Simulations on phylogenetic trees and hierarchical clustering show the method gives accurate p-values where naive bootstrap fails.

No. A chain of gears can't send signals faster than light, and in practice it's way slower than electricity or light in fiber.

Reason: gears aren't perfectly rigid. When you push the first gear, that push travels as a compression wave—tooth by tooth. Each gear has to bend slightly and push the next one. That wave moves at the speed of sound in the material. For steel, that's around 5,000 m/s. Light travels at 300,000,000 m/s. So you're looking at tens of thousands of times slower.

Same thing with a really long rod. If you could push a light-year-long rod, the other end wouldn't move instantly. The push gets there after years because information travels at sound speed in the rod.

Then there's all the practical stuff—backlash, friction, slack—which makes real systems even slower. Plus relativity says nothing can send information faster than light anyway, period. No way around it.

Saturday night, 9:40 p.m. Scrubs in the hamper. Coffee's cold. I'm sitting on the kitchen floor with my back against the dishwasher because sitting in chairs feels too exposed.

They're all here like always. Mrs. Delgado by the fridge in her hospital gown, hands folded the way they were on the table. She doesn't speak. The boy from last spring—bicycle accident—sits by the window bouncing a ball that makes no sound.

I thought I'd make peace with it eventually. Everyone tells you that. You can't save everyone. You did everything right. I know I did everything right. But knowing doesn't empty the room.

So I cook anyway. Eggs, toast. The kind of meal that doesn't ask anything of you. I set out an extra plate. I've never explained that to anyone. It's not for them exactly. It's so the table doesn't feel like an accusation.

'I'm sorry,' I tell the room like I always do. It's my Saturday ritual, like washing hands before surgery.

Tonight something shifts. Mrs. Delgado unfolds her hands. She walks to the kitchen and very slowly lifts the plate and sets it in front of the boy. He stops bouncing the ball. He looks at the toast, then at me, and for a second he almost smiles.

I don't breathe. Nobody moves.

Then he picks up the toast. He can't eat it but he holds it like something precious. The others drift closer one at a time until the kitchen is full of people with nothing to say and nowhere else to be.

I sit with them until midnight, saying all their names out loud because somebody should.

When I finally stand my knees ache, eyes burn, but my hands are steady. Monday I scrub in at seven. I'll try again. It's the only apology I know how to make.

text:
Daniel Whitmore was six years old the first time he saw the woman, standing on a pier in Lisbon with melting ice cream and a sunburned nose. She was sitting on a bench, wearing a deep blue dress, reading. She looked up once. He waved. She smiled but didn't wave back, then disappeared into the crowd.

He didn't think about it until next summer, a mountain village in Switzerland. There she was on a balcony across the street in a blue coat even though it was hot. He told his mom. She laughed, said lots of people wear blue.

Years went by. More sightings. Blue scarf at a market in Marrakesh. Blue umbrella at a train station in Kyoto. Blue silk shawl at the back of a church in Florence. She never approached. Never seemed to age. Daniel kept a notebook—started as a game, turned into something close to obsession. By fifteen he had nine sightings across nine countries. His dad said gently that maybe he was seeing what he wanted to see.

He thought about that seriously. He was rational, knew the mind seeks patterns. But the details bothered him. The shade of blue never changed. Her expression—calm, faintly amused—never changed. And she was always looking directly at him.

Eighteenth birthday dinner in Genoa, overlooking the harbor. Daniel was distracted, scanning the room like usual. When dessert came his mom tapped her glass.

'There's someone we want you to meet. We should've done this years ago.'

A door opened. The woman in blue walked toward them, older now, maybe sixty, silver hair, same calm expression. Daniel stood up, couldn't speak.

'This is Margaret Ellison,' his father said. 'She was your grandmother's closest friend. Your grandmother made us promise we'd introduce you when you turned eighteen.'

Margaret put out her hand. 'I'm sorry for the secrecy. Your grandmother wanted me to watch over you as you grew. She thought you should discover the world for yourself but never be entirely alone.'

Marta knew something was wrong before she even opened her eyes. The pillow smelled like her shampoo but when she touched her jaw there was stubble, and her hand—held up in the gray light—was broad, thick-knuckled. Her father's hand. When she said 'oh,' the sound came from deep in her chest and rattled the glass on the nightstand.

By eight o'clock everyone knew. Her neighbor Mrs. Lindqvist, seventy-four, was laughing this deep baritone through the wall. Marta stood in the bathroom staring at a stranger. Six feet tall. Shoulders that filled the mirror. She flexed and watched the muscle jump.

She'd wanted a body like this for years.

Dale was six-two. He didn't need to hit her often—once was enough to teach her the apartment geography. Which corners were safe. Which floorboards creaked. How long to the door. She'd made herself small in every room he walked into. Even after the divorce she kept a packed bag under the sink and a chair wedged under the doorknob.

Dale was somewhere in the city waking up smaller than she was now.

She waited to feel triumphant. What she felt was her new heart hammering.

Three knocks at the door at noon, spaced the way he always did. Her whole body went cold. Through the peephole a small woman, Dale's pale eyes, hands up, palms out. 'Marta. I just want to talk. Look at me. You've got nothing to be afraid of.'

Marta backed against the wall. Her arms could lift the door off its hinges. She was shaking so hard her teeth clicked.

That's when she got it: the fear had never lived in her muscles. It lived in the knowing. In what he'd do when the door was closed. Her body changed overnight. The fear didn't even notice.

'I'm still afraid of you,' she said through the wood, in her father's voice. 'I want you to hear that. I'm the strongest I've ever been and I'm still afraid of you. That's what you did.'

Silence. Then, thin and sharp: 'Don't be dramatic.'

Sharp sounded the same in any voice. Footsteps went down the stairs, light and quick.

A softer knock a minute later. 'Marta? It's Edna Lindqvist. I heard through the wall. Police are on the way and I'm sitting right here until they come.'

She opened the door. On the landing sat a stout old man in a flowered robe. She lowered herself onto the step beside him—two strangers in borrowed bodies—and waited. Her hands had finally stopped shaking.

Should Companies Track Employee Online Activity?

Employers want to know what happens on their networks. Employees want privacy. I think companies should be able to monitor online activity at work, but with real limits.

Start with security. Company networks hold customer records, financial data, trade secrets. One employee clicks a bad link or uploads to a personal account and it's all exposed. Monitoring catches that early. Companies are legally responsible for what happens on their systems—harassment, data leaks—so they need to detect misconduct. And honestly, a company pays for working hours so it's fair to check those hours are being used for work.

But unlimited surveillance is harmful. Constant monitoring stresses people out and makes them distrustful. Research shows stressed employees are often less productive, not more. It also digs into private stuff—messages, medical searches, union organizing—things workers should keep to themselves. And data collected for security can get repurposed.

The answer is regulated monitoring. Tell employees what's tracked and why, in writing, before you start. Monitor work accounts and devices, not personal ones. Collect only what you need. Store it securely. Focus on risk patterns instead of reading every message.

With safeguards, monitoring protects both the business and workers. Without them, it turns a workplace into a place where nobody trusts anyone.

The devil's office smelled like burnt coffee and old paperwork. Not what Daniel expected.

'Sit,' the devil said. He looked like a tired accountant in a gray cardigan. 'Résumé?'

'Wait, I thought this was a different job,' Daniel said. Mid-level compliance officer from Dayton. Vague email about an opportunity.

'It is. Mine.' The devil slid a folder over. 'Six thousand years. I'm tired. The lake of fire needs maintenance, demons are unionizing, humanity's gotten so inventive I barely do anything anymore. You people don't need the help.'

Daniel opened it. Seven headshots. All stamped REJECTED in red.

'What was wrong with them?'

'Too eager.' The devil rubbed his eyes. 'First one cackled during the interview. Another wanted to know if he'd get a throne. A third wanted to rule. None of them understood the job is mostly paperwork.'

'Paperwork?'

'Souls. Intake, categorization, appeals.' The devil looked exhausted. 'Everyone thinks I tempt them. Mostly I just file.'

Daniel thought about his own desk, his stack of forms. His manager once said without irony that rules separated people from chaos.

'What's the salary?'

'Eternal.'

'Benefits?'

'Corner office. Unlimited dental—hell's hard on teeth.' The devil leaned forward. 'And you can reject anyone you like. That's the secret perk. Nobody tells you that part.'

'Reject?' Daniel said slowly. 'Like, deny entry?'

'To the worst ones. The ones who really deserve to be in the wrong place.' The devil looked sad. 'Six thousand years being the only one who could say no. Gets lonely.'

Daniel looked at the folder again. Every person who'd cut a corner, lied on a form, smiled while stealing. Every one whose paperwork he'd had to approve.

'One question,' he said.

'Yeah?'

'Is there a handbook?'

The devil smiled for the first time. For a second he looked relieved.

'Oh,' he said, 'you're going to be terrifying.'

From the ridge, Fort Knox looked almost peaceful. Eighty years of kudzu had swallowed the barracks. The old depository sat in the middle like a gray tooth. Only the turrets spoiled it. Four on the corners, swinging in slow patient arcs. Dying sun flashing off the lenses each time they turned.

Marisol lowered her binoculars. 'Still running.'

'Solar,' Dutch whispered. He was an electrician before the collapse, talked about circuits like other people talked about God. 'Panels on every roof, batteries in the bunkers. Nobody ever told the system to stop.'

Five of them left Louisville with a story: a vault of gold bars stacked like firewood. Untouched. Enough to buy a kingdom. The story didn't mention the sentry drones on the Bardstown road. Didn't mention the wire that cut Pell and Okafor in half when they walked up to look at the gate. A machine that'd never been told the war ended.

Three left now. Marisol, Dutch, and Teo, fifteen, hasn't spoken since the fence.

'The optics are the weak point,' Dutch said. 'When the sun drops behind that ridge the glare blinds the north lens. Ninety seconds. Maybe less.'

'Maybe less?'

'I never said it was good.'

They ran at dusk. Grass whipped Marisol's knees. Teo's boots pounded behind her in rhythm with her heart. Fifty yards from the wall a servo whined. The north turret swung toward them, hesitated, found only glare.

Then the east turret woke up.

Rounds chewed the earth. Dutch shoved Teo into a ditch, Marisol dove after. When she raised her head Dutch was standing in the open swinging a battered camp radio over his head until it screamed static. The east turret turned.

'Go!' he shouted.

The gun answered.

She didn't remember crossing the last hundred feet. Remembered Teo's hand, cold steel of the vault door, a speaker crackling above the keypad.

'Unauthorized access detected. Treasury Police have been notified. Please state your business.'

Her mouth was dust. 'We're here for the gold.'

'Withdrawals require Form 27-B and an appointment with the Secretary. Your request has been forwarded. Please hold.'

The doors rolled open. The turrets went silent. Through every speaker a tinny cheerful piano started playing.

The gold was real. Neat endless stacks. Each bar stamped, numbered, worth more than lives spent crossing Kentucky. Marisol lifted one. Twenty-seven pounds. You couldn't eat it or burn it or plant it.

Teo picked up a bar. Spoke for the first time in three days. 'Dutch would've wanted us to take it.'

They carried out what they could while the machine waited, patiently, on hold for a Secretary who would never answer.

The first thing Marguerite did after the funeral was eat a whole sleeve of good crackers standing at the counter because nobody was there to tell her that wasn't dinner.

Second thing was her brother's email. Four lines. 'Mom's house sells next month. Thought you should know. No need to come. Hope you're okay.' Just an initial. Like she was a client.

Fifty-three. Forgotten for about eleven months by her count. Her husband faded slow, then the layoff, then friends stopped calling because grief was contagious apparently. Somewhere in there she started doing math on pills in the cabinet. Not seriously. Just math.

Tonight the math was loud.

She opened the cabinet. Looked at the orange bottles a long time. Then at the fridge where a postcard was pinned from her sister-in-law Delia who at the funeral said loudly, in front of everyone: 'Well, Marguerite always did take things hard.'

Always did take things hard. Like she was a houseplant.

Marguerite closed the cabinet.

Nothing had lifted. She wanted to be clear about that. The grief sat in her chest like a stone in a river and the water just kept going around it. But something small and mean and stubborn woke up under the stone.

If she were gone Delia would tell the story at Thanksgiving with a sad head tilt. 'Poor Marguerite. We should have seen.' Make it about herself. Her brother would sell the house and feel a clean sad feeling.

No.

She got a pen. On the back of Delia's postcard under her loopy handwriting she wrote: Day one. Then the date. Then: Out of spite.

Not a beautiful reason. She knew that. There were better ones, gentler ones, the kind therapists put on posters. Maybe she'd find one eventually.

But spite got her off the couch. Spite made her put the pills away. Spite, she thought, taking the last cracker, might get her to the doctor Monday.

She'd go to the doctor. Answer the phone when her cousin called. Plant tomatoes in spring if only so she could invite everyone to watch her enjoy them.

Stay alive very much on purpose, the most irritating way possible.

One day maybe she'd forget why she started.

It stood open in the sand at the tree line like a flag. Before I touched it I knew: the bent rib on the left, the initials I'd scratched in sixth grade with a house key. Lost it on a train eleven years earlier and mourned it for a week. My mother bought it. I closed it. The fabric still smelled like her hallway.

Past the umbrella the beach rose into a dune and I stopped. The dune was socks. Thousands of them, sun-bleached, drifting like pale leaves. Beyond them a field of pens. A slope of sunglasses. A long glittering hillside of keys: house keys, car keys, a tiny brass one that locked my diary when I was nine. Organized like a lost-property office, by category.

First thought was practical. A world's lost things should have a knife. Dug through keys for an hour. Found my father's garage flashlight. A thermos from a ski trip. Finally the red pocketknife I dropped at summer camp when I was twelve. Blade still sharp.

By dusk I had fire, a knife, growing unease. The island kept opening like a drawer. My grandfather's watch on a flat rock, ticking, set to some right time somewhere. My first dog's collar hanging from a branch. Overdue library books stacked under a palm.

In the grass by the fire: a red mitten with a hole in the thumb. Belonged to a girl named Priya in fourth grade who lent it when my hands went numb at the bus stop. I lost it on the way home, never told her. Thirty years later I sat holding it and apologized to the empty beach out loud.

Fifth day, far shore, cliffs dropped to a cove. I reached what I'd been avoiding. A gray rowboat half in the surf. In it, whittling a stick, was a man in a green cardigan dead six years. My father. He looked up. 'There you are. Wondered how long it'd take.'

'Am I dead?' I asked.

'Don't be dramatic. You're just late. Everything lost waits until somebody remembers to get it.'

Overhead, a faint mechanical hum had started—the sound I gave up on by day three. My father nodded at the sky. 'That's yours. You can only carry what you can hold. Choose.'

I took the umbrella because the sky had darkened and because it was my mother's. At the waterline I turned to wave but the cove was empty. Boat, cardigan, the whole bright hillside of keys. Only rain remained. I opened the umbrella, held it over my head, waited for the plane to find me.
